sections.html:
Assessing and collecting happen in two adjoining buildings on Crimson Laurel Circle in Bakersville. Hours for both are 8:00 to 4:30, Monday to Friday.

  • Assessor: Suite 5 at number 26, phone 828.688.2139 extension 1407. Staff list, value and assess real and personal property.
  • Collector: number 61, phone 828.537.1627. Staff mail the bills and accept payment.

The assessor also takes applications for relief, exemptions, exclusions and Present Use Value. Seven fire districts levy a tax that the collector adds to the bill, so what you owe depends partly on where your parcel lies.

sections.h2: Mitchell County housing at a glance
sections.html:
About 15,062 people lived in Mitchell County in July 2025, up slightly from 14,903 in 2020. The county has 8,785 housing units. Owners occupy 76.3 percent of them. The survey for 2020 to 2024 puts the middle home value at $220,100 and the middle rent at $813. Builders took out 44 permits in 2025.

Older owners are a large group here, with 27.6 percent of residents 65 or over, so the relief programs described below come up often.

Bills fall due September 1, and no interest is added until after January 5. On January 6 the account turns delinquent and 2 percent is added, followed by 0.75 percent for every further month. A deadline on a Saturday or Sunday rolls to Monday.

Mitchell County tax year
Time of yearStep
January 1Assessment date
JanuaryListing month for changes
JulyCurrent bills processed
AugustBills mailed to January 1 owner of record
September 1Payment due
January 5Last interest-free day
FebruaryDelinquent notices go out
MarchDelinquent list advertised

State law behind the interest-free cutoff is G.S. 105-360.

Walk-in payers at the Tax Office may use cash, a check, or a debit or credit card. The county's online portal, at mitchell.webtaxpay.com, accepts cards and e-checks, and the vendor that runs it keeps a convenience fee.

Current taxes can be paid in monthly installments. Late balances can be spread out too, once you sign a payment agreement. If you are already behind, call 828.537.1627 before the March newspaper advertisement.

August bills are addressed to the January 1 owner of record. If you sold in, say, June, your name is still the one on the envelope, so make sure the closing papers show who handled that year.

Changes to land, buildings or taxable personal property are reported during January. The commissioners can extend that window, and property listed late carries a 10 percent penalty. The authority is G.S. 105-307.

Taxable items include:

  • business assets,
  • untagged vehicles,
  • boats and personal watercraft,
  • untagged campers and trailers,
  • mobile homes,
  • aircraft.

Print the forms from the state revenue department, complete them and mail them to Suite 5. New construction, a removed outbuilding or a newly placed manufactured home are all worth reporting.

Value complaints go to the equalization board, which is the county commissioners unless a separate panel has been appointed. Under G.S. 105-322 it holds its first meeting no sooner than the first Monday in April and no later than the first Monday in May.

  • Ask to be heard, by letter or at the office, before the board adjourns.
  • When a notice goes out fewer than 15 days before adjournment, your deadline is 15 days after it was mailed.
  • The board mails its ruling no later than 30 days after it adjourns.
  • To go on to the Property Tax Commission, file within 30 days (G.S. 105-290).

Real estate has to be reappraised every eight years at most, and in those years the board remains in session through December 1. Phone the assessor to learn when your parcel was last revalued and when the next round is due.

Each owner may claim one of three state programs. The application is Form AV-9, filed with the assessor.

  • Age or disability exclusion: an exclusion of $25,000 or half the value, if that is higher. Owners must be 65 or older, or permanently disabled, with 2026 income at or under $38,800.
  • Disabled veteran exclusion: $45,000 is excluded from value, and age and income are not tested. Start by completing Form NCDVA-9 with a veteran service officer.
  • Circuit breaker: once you have lived in the home five years, the bill is capped at 4 percent of income, or 5 percent when 2026 income runs up to $58,200. Reapply each year.

Anything deferred under the circuit breaker is owed once the house is sold or no longer lived in, so sellers need the deferred total from the assessor. The statute is G.S. 105-277.1B.

Phone the Tax Collector first, at 828.537.1627. Request the amount due for this year and any earlier year, and find out whether an installment plan or payment agreement is running. An estimate will not do; your closing attorney needs the payoff in writing.

Next, call the assessor at extension 1407 and ask whether the parcel carries an exclusion or a deferred circuit breaker balance, since a deferral comes due at transfer. Collect your own papers too: the latest bill, any AV-9 you submitted, and your deed.

If you added buildings or finished new work, confirm those additions are on the record before a buyer's appraiser sees them.

sections.h2: What happens at the closing table
sections.html:
Taxes are one line among many on the settlement statement, and a few habits keep it clean.

  • Give the attorney the written payoff from the collector at least a few days before closing.
  • Settle who covers the bill mailed in August to the January 1 owner.
  • Hand over the assessor's answer on exclusions or deferred circuit breaker tax, so those amounts are counted.
  • Once the sale closes, tell the assessor where the next bill should go.

A bill that is already delinquent can still be paid out of proceeds, which is often simpler than negotiating a payment agreement while a sale is pending.

On the January 1 listing date a lien attaches, and penalties and costs get added to it (G.S. 105-355). If the county sues under G.S. 105-374 the case ends at a courthouse-door auction.

That process takes time. Three days after the sale the commissioner files a report, and raised bids or objections have 10 days from that report. An owner may still redeem before the court confirms, by paying taxes, penalty, interest and costs. Selling first keeps the price in your hands.

A seller here can handle this in three moves: get a payoff from the collector, ask the assessor about relief or a deferral on the parcel, and pass both figures to the closing attorney. Where repairs are out of reach, a written as-is cash offer can fit that timeline.

faqs.q: When does interest begin on a Mitchell County bill?
faqs.a: January 6. The final interest-free day is January 5. After that the charge is 2 percent for the first month and 0.75 percent for every later month.

faqs.q: Where is the walk-in payment counter?
faqs.a: At the Tax Collector's counter, 61 Crimson Laurel Circle in Bakersville, any weekday between 8:00 and 4:30. It takes cash, checks, and debit or credit cards.

faqs.q: Who answers questions on my assessment or exemption form?
faqs.a: The Tax Assessor handles both, at 828.688.2139 extension 1407. The office is at 26 Crimson Laurel Circle, Suite 5.

faqs.q: May I pay my bill in installments?
faqs.a: Yes, in monthly payments on the current year's tax. Late balances qualify too once you sign a payment agreement.

faqs.q: What happens if I forget to list property in January?
faqs.a: A 10 percent penalty is added. The regular window is the month of January unless the commissioners extend it.
